prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms confined in a magic-wavelength lattice are interrogated free of light-shift, Doppler and recoil errors, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B052 as the sole prize with Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. Having read all eight statements and the chair's questions, I find that no member disputes the physics or the roughly 1e-18 performance, and that every objection is about overlap, timing or credit. On overlap, which is the chair's first question, the physical difference from the 2005 and 2012 prizes can be stated in one sentence. The comb made optical cycles countable, and the ion-control work showed that a single, isolated quantum system can serve as a clock. Neither gave a way to hold thousands of neutral atoms with no first-order Doppler or recoil shift and with the light shift of the clock transition cancelled at once. That is what the magic-wavelength condition inside a Lamb-Dicke lattice does. It moves the limit from the statistics of one ion to the systematics of an ensemble, and it is why stability and accuracy improved together, not one at the expense of the other. The consequence is also a physics result and not only a tool: clocks at this level resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres, bound drifts of fundamental constants and open searches for ultralight dark matter. I would therefore want the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 demonstration, and I have rewritten it that way, so that Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson can read it as a distinct step. On timing, I still see no reason to tie a prize to an administrative decision on the SI second; the confirmed physics does not change when that decision is taken. Finally, the two-name credit is the least contested on the shortlist, as the chair's summary also records.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson share: that the clock is the third prize in one precision-spectroscopy lineage and that a conceptually broader candidate such as B044 or B021 would be the larger step. I do not think this is answered by the physics alone, so I accept that the committee is making a judgement about the kind of achievement it wants to honour, and a member who weighs conceptual breadth over measurement reach could reasonably rank the clocks lower. Second, the credit does leave out real contributors. Takamoto's strontium demonstration and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST accuracy and comparison results are not covered, and Lindroth is right that the citation has to be tied to the lattice scheme and its record demonstrations, not to optical clocks in general. Third, the claim in my citation about a 10^-18 level relies on my recollection of the literature and not on a verified source in this file. Last, I again note my own bias toward measurement-limited advances, and my committee colleagues are right to discount for it.

responses.point: Mehlig regards B044 as qualitatively a new class of many-body experiments and the clock as a superb instrument and an improvement in precision; he has moved B052 up to his first alternative and says he would be comfortable with either if attribution certainty is preferred.
responses.response: I appreciate that you moved the clock up, and I think we are closer than the opening ranking suggested. Where we still differ is on whether the clock is only an improvement in precision. A factor of order 100 in accuracy that comes from a new trapping scheme and that for the first time lets one compare parts of a single sample at millimetre separations is a change in what can be measured, which is the same kind of argument you make for the quantum gas microscope. On B044 itself my difficulty is the one you state yourself: Zoller, Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger cannot be fitted into three places without a painful omission, and Zoller also sits on B009. I kept B044 as my first alternative because I value the science, but the credit problem there is real and the clock does not have it. If you still see a physics objection to B052 beyond overlap and timing, the chair has asked you to state it, and I would like to hear it.

responses.point: Eriksson sees the lattice clock as an incremental advance in a field already honoured in 2005 and 2012, regards a new class of matter (B021) as the larger conceptual step, and thinks the redefinition of the second is a reason to wait slightly, though he would accept B052 without objection if clean credit is preferred.
responses.response: Your acceptance of B052 if credit is the deciding factor matters to me, and I think the committee should say that it is. On the conceptual step, I would put it this way: a new class of matter is a discovery about what a material can be, whereas the lattice clock is a discovery about how to remove every first-order error from a measurement of a transition frequency, and the statutes allow either. I also think the credit problem you yourself describe for B021, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang left out of a prize whose experimental half they motivated, is more serious than anything attached to the clock, and I am not able to judge it as you can. On waiting, I would reverse your argument: a prize for the clock does not depend on the SI decision, whereas waiting does carry a cost in a field where several groups now report at the same level and the credit picture will only get more crowded. If a condensed-matter citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant can be drawn so that the omission is defensible, that is for you and Lindroth to judge, and I would not stand in its way in a later year.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the measurement-enabling criterion I apply to the clock cuts at least as sharply for aberration correction in B011, and that the pending redefinition of the second is a timing argument that applies to B052 and not to an instrument used for twenty years.
responses.response: I agree that the criterion is the same and that B011 is a mature and clearly attributable invention, so I accept the symmetry and would not call your candidate a poor prize. Where I still separate them is on what the achievement does to physics. Aberration correction extends our ability to image structure, and its main effect is through materials science and chemistry; the lattice clock changes the sensitivity of tests of gravity and of constants, so it enters physics itself. You also raise credit, and there I agree it is cleaner for you than for most: a corrector is an object three people made work. But the STEM lineage of Krivanek and Dellby is outside your three names, and I can only treat that as a limit I cannot judge from the files. On timing, the redefinition is not a precondition for the lattice clock as a discovery, and I do not think that it delays the award in the way you suggest; the confirmed physics is what is being recognised. I will keep the thorium clock out of the citation, as I said, so Ye's work on it does not bear on this.

responses.point: Johansson holds that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits is a separable achievement from circuit QED and should be a tie-breaker at most, and he accepts B052 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I accept the correction. The 2025 prize and the 2004 architecture are different conceptual steps and I should not have let community overlap stand in for a judgement of merit; I used it as a sequencing argument and I hold it only that way. My remaining reasons for ranking circuit QED below the clock are the four names for three places, which you also say you cannot defend on scientific grounds, and my view that a good part of its strength is as quantum-computing engineering. I also note that you propose Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin and that Blais versus Girvin cannot be settled here. If the committee decides it wants a circuits prize, your suggestion of tying it to the experimental realisation is a good one, and I would not oppose it as a later prize. Given your disclosure of field proximity, I also agree that the chair should decide on recusal for B056, but that is not my decision.

responses.point: Lindroth agrees on the structure of the credit but cautions that Takamoto, PTB, SYRTE and NIST and the earlier laser-stabilisation work mean the credit is clean for the lattice-clock concept and performance record, not for every clock result, and asks that the citation be narrow.
responses.response: I take that on fully and have changed the wording of my citation to follow it: it names the magic-wavelength lattice and the interrogation free of light-shift, Doppler and recoil errors, and it says nothing about optical clocks in general. As an atomic physicist you are better placed than I am on the stability and systematic budget, and I would ask you whether the case for crediting Ye for the 1e-18 record rather than for a general programme of precision spectroscopy holds up for the evidence we have. I also note that I defer to you on the early priority details.

uncertainties: Whether the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes will be read as complementary or incremental by Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson; this depends on how the citation is framed and I cannot settle it for them.
Whether the committee will wait for the formal redefinition of the second; I do not think the physics requires it but it is a committee judgement.
Whether credit beyond Katori and Ye (Takamoto, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) will be thought necessary; the shortlist offers no third name and priority details here are recalled from memory.
If B052 is not carried, the choice between B044, with Zoller or Esslinger as the third name, and B009, with its 2012 overlap and Zoller in both candidates, remains open for me.
Whether my disclosed connection to the Hall laboratory is regarded as requiring recusal on B052.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory during my doctoral period, and Jun Ye trained and worked in the Hall group at JILA. This is a shared background in one laboratory environment and not a collaboration or supervisory relationship; I have no documented co-authorship with Katori or Ye. I also work in laser spectroscopy and coherent light-matter interaction, and Lund colleagues work in neighbouring areas. I have flagged this in round 1 and ask the chair and the committee to decide whether it requires recusal for B052. I will accept their decision, and I would give no weight in my argument to the connection. No other specific conflict is apparent from my profile.
